questions.explanation: Value is measured as a gain or a loss against a reference point, and the marginal change is worth less the further it sits from that point. A gain of a hundred dollars from a reference of zero is felt differently from the same sum gained from a reference ten times as high, and a loss of a hundred dollars from a higher reference is felt less keenly than the same loss from a lower one. The reference point is set by the person's own situation, which is why two people can face identical final wealth and react in opposite ways.
questions.hint: Ask whether the slope of the value function is constant as the outcome moves away from the reference.

options.text: A person values final wealth rather than the change from the reference point
options.misconception: treats the outcome as a level rather than as a change

questions.explanation: For a loss the second branch applies, so the magnitude is 2.2 times the square root of the loss. The square root of 100 is 10, and multiplying by 2.2 gives 22, so v(-100) = -22. The gain of the same size is worth only 10, which is the loss aversion built into the coefficient. The result is a negative number, as every loss must be, because the value function is signed relative to the reference point.

questions.explanation: The magnitudes are 22 for the loss and 10 for the gain, and the loss aversion coefficient is the ratio of the two, which is 22 over 10, or 2.2. A coefficient above one is what makes the value function steeper on the loss side, and it is the single most consequential departure from expected utility: a person facing an even-money choice will refuse the gamble. The same coefficient also makes people resist selling what they own, since giving it up turns a gain into zero and throws away value.

questions.explanation: The square root makes the value function concave above the reference point, so the marginal value of a dollar declines as the gain rises. That is diminishing sensitivity, and the two steps here are equal in width but unequal in value, which is exactly what concavity requires. The mirror image holds below the reference point, where the loss branch is convex, so an additional slice of loss costs less than an equal slice nearer the reference. Both halves together give the familiar S shape.

questions.explanation: Four portfolios are available. Holding both is worth 5 plus -11, which is -6. Selling the loser and keeping the winner is worth 5. Selling the winner and keeping the loser is worth -11, and selling both is worth zero. The highest is 5, so the value function says sell the loser, and that is exactly the disposition effect: gains are realised promptly and losses are held. The rule is not irrational in its own terms, since -6 is worse than 5, but it leaves the portfolio in the holdings that look worst on paper.

questions.explanation: Selling the winners keeps the holdings that have fallen and sells the holdings that have risen, so the portfolio is left concentrated in the assets whose reference-dependent value is worst. A portfolio that has been pruned this way is not the portfolio that a buy-and-hold investor would hold, and its returns are systematically below the returns of the market it came from. The transaction costs and tax effects make the habit worse, but they are additions to the cost rather than its source; the source is that the sale is chosen by reference to the purchase price rather than to the current value.

questions.explanation: A mental account is a bookkeeping device with its own budget, and a purchase is judged against the balance of the account it comes from rather than against total resources. Money is therefore not fungible in the consumer's head, which allows a category to be run down past the point where the overall budget would have stopped it, and the temptation to dip into another category is resisted even though the money is identical. The effect is strongest when the transfer between accounts is visible, as with a gift card or a holiday fund, because the consumer can see the balance fall.

questions.explanation: The buyer pays 50000 dollars against a reservation value of 45000, so the anchor extracts 5000 dollars above what the buyer would have paid. The distance from the reservation value to the anchor is 15000 dollars, so the share that survives is 5000 over 15000, which is one third. The measure matters because it is scale free: a second deal anchored 30000 dollars higher, with the same ratio of concession, would extract twice as much, which is what a negotiator is trying to arrange.

The weighting is more than double the true probability, so a one in ten chance is treated as though it were one in four. The same function weights a probability of nine tenths at three quarters, so it overstates small chances and understates large ones, which is the inverse-S shape that the certainty and doubt effects both require.

The positive results therefore number one thousand and eighty, of which ninety are genuine, and the probability is ninety over one thousand and eighty, which is one twelfth, or about 0.0833. The false share is nine hundred and ninety over one thousand and eighty, which is eleven twelfths, or about 0.9167. The two figures are complements of each other, so the true share is one twelfth, and most positive results in a rare condition are false however good the test looks.

questions.explanation: In the described urn the probabilities are known and the choice is a matter of expected value, while in the other urn the subject must supply the probabilities himself. If he assigns a probability to red on the described urn that differs from the one he assigns to the other urn, the two subjective probabilities cannot both be correct, and the pair violates independence: the chance of red must be the same in either urn if the composition alone decides. A preference for the known urn is therefore not a preference for less risk, since a subject could hold a subjective belief that red is more likely there and still decline the gamble.

questions.explanation: Today's discount takes the price to 200 less 40, which is 160 dollars, and the discount in 30 days takes it to 200 less 50, which is 150 dollars. The two discounted prices differ by only 10 dollars, so the shopper faces a very small price change spread over a month. Under exponential discounting a small per-period rate is worth very little over 30 days, and the shopper waits; under hyperbolic discounting the difference between now and 30 days is large relative to the difference between 30 and 60 days, and the shopper buys at once. questions.explanation: The weight on a sum arriving in a month is the amount taken now divided by the amount offered later. In the first comparison that is 15 over 30, which is one half, so the small sum is discounted heavily. In the second it is 90 over 105, which is six sevenths, or about 0.857, so the large sum is barely discounted at all. A single discount rate cannot produce both figures, and the direction of the difference is diagnostic: present bias always makes the weight rise with the size of the sum, so a small gain loses a larger share to impatience than a large one.
questions.hint: Divide the amount taken now by the amount offered later, and repeat for the second pair.

questions.explanation: The first month carries the whole factor of 0.9, giving a weight of 0.9, and the second month multiplies by 0.9 again, giving 0.81. What matters is not the level but the shape: the first month costs 0.1 of weight and the second costs 0.09, nine tenths of the first, and each later month costs a little less again. The function is therefore steep at the present and progressively flatter, which is what produces short-run impatience and long-run patience in the same person.
questions.hint: Multiply the one-off factor by the per-month factor raised to the number of months.

questions.explanation: Present bias creates a problem of self-control rather than of information: the person knows the saving is right and will still prefer to spend when the moment arrives. A binding commitment works by removing the option rather than by improving the terms, which is why a modest penalty or an automatic transfer can change behaviour where advice does not. questions.explanation: The restraint bias is the observation that the more a person denies themselves, the more they want the denied item afterwards, and the desire is larger than it would have been without the denial. It is not an explanation in terms of calories or of a physiological rebound, and it is not present bias, which is about comparing across time rather than about desire depending on a prior episode. The practical consequence is that a plan relying on repeated small denials can raise total intake, so the design has to remove the temptation rather than require the refusal.

questions.explanation: Under certainty a price known to be lower tomorrow is strictly better, so a rational buyer waits and the option value of waiting is positive. What removes it is a belief rather than a risk preference: if the price might rise sharply, buying now is a hedge and the expected saving must be weighed against the possibility of paying much more. A present-biased buyer overstates the saving from waiting because it lands soon and feels vivid, while the possibility of a large increase is discounted, so both mistakes push in the same direction and the buyer acts as though certainty held.

questions.explanation: Automatic enrolment turns inaction into a decision, and most people prefer to do nothing when the decision carries any effort or any risk of regret. The participation rate is therefore set by the default rather than by a comparison of plans, which is why reversing the default changes participation by a large factor with no change in either plan. The mechanism is weak adherence, not a belief that the default plan is best, and it is strongest where the consequences of the default are hard to assess at the moment of choice.

questions.explanation: A decoy is dominated on every attribute, so a chooser comparing attributes should never pick it, and its presence cannot make it attractive. What it does is change the comparison among the remaining options: the middle option now looks better value than the cheapest one, because the cheapest is no longer the smallest outlay on offer. The share taken by the middle option rises, and the total profit of the firm rises with it, which is why the device is used despite leaving the assortment on offer worse for some choosers.

questions.explanation: Asymmetric dominance holds when one option is at least as good on the attribute the chooser cares about and strictly better on the other, so choosing against it requires a preference for the attribute the chooser has said matters less. questions.explanation: Duration neglect says the remembered quality of an episode is close to insensitive to its length once the peak and the final moment are held fixed, which follows from the same weighting the peak-end rule imposes. It is a serious design problem wherever a service is experienced repeatedly, because a provider can improve the recollection of an episode by lengthening the ending rather than by improving the whole experience. It also means that a long ordeal endured with a tolerable ending can be remembered less badly than a short one that ended badly.

The finding is that a larger assortment can lower the rate at which anything is bought, because the extra comparisons raise the cost of working out which option to take and some shoppers end up buying nothing at all. The mechanism is a decision cost rather than a change in taste, so it is strongest for shoppers who know little about the products and weakest for those who can evaluate them quickly.
questions.hint: Subtract the two rates, which are already expressed in percentage points.
questions.learningObjective: compute the difference in purchase rate across assortment sizes

questions.explanation: Half of 100 dollars is 50, so a share of 50 is the smallest the responder will take and anything below it is rejected, returning the whole pie to the proposer. The incentive threshold is therefore a half. What the experiments find is that proposers typically offer materially less than a half and that such offers are frequently accepted, so the share actually taken in equilibrium is below the level the responder's stated rule implies. The gap is the descriptive fact; the rule is the incentive fact.

questions.explanation: A receiver who was sent nothing has no reason to return anything, and a receiver who was sent a positive sum returns a positive amount far more often than the incentives alone would produce. The response is highest in the first encounter with a sender who has previously sent, so the pattern is conditional on being treated well rather than a general preference for giving. Two consequences follow: a one-shot game sustains less trust than a repeated one, and an individual's reputation for sending raises what it pays to send, which is why the behaviour survives in repeated play.

questions.explanation: If all three pick the same number, the average is that number and the target is two thirds of it, so the number is closest to itself exactly when it equals the target, which forces it to be zero. The argument is about levels rather than about marginal incentives: any guess above zero can be lowered to win the same pot more often, so numbers above zero are eliminated one after another, and the only guess that survives is the bottom of the range. Asking for a high number is asking for a target that everyone else will also try to beat, which is why rational play collapses to the floor.
questions.hint: Set the common guess equal to two thirds of itself, since the average of identical guesses is that guess.

questions.explanation: The first two offers fall short of the 40 dollar standard, so they are passed over, and the 45 dollar offer clears it and is taken, even though the 60 dollar offer arrives afterwards. The cost of stopping is therefore 60 minus 45, which is 15 dollars, and that is the whole price of the rule. The rule is worth it whenever the cost of examining one more offer exceeds the expected gain, which is why the value of continued search falls as the searcher approaches the end of the list.

questions.explanation: Inside a firm the information needed to rank projects is held by the project teams, and what reaches the centre is a report rather than the underlying facts. When the report cannot be checked, the selection rule is a rule about reporting, so the outcome reflects who can present best rather than which project earns most. The response is to make the underlying data observable, which is the same logic as a disclosure rule or an outside auditor: the cost of verification has to be set against the cost of acting on an unverifiable report.

questions.explanation: Slack is the difference between the resources a holder is given and the resources the holder thinks are needed, and it is discretionary whenever the holder is not observed on the output the resources produce. A budget-only measure makes the slack look like good performance, so the holder has a reason to hold back and the reason disappears if output is also measured. The problem is therefore the measurement design rather than the holder's motives, and it disappears when the two are combined, since a holder who wants output and wants to be under budget has little slack to hide.
questions.hint: Ask what the measure rewards and what it leaves unobserved.

questions.explanation: A calibrated forecaster making 25 statements of 60 percent confidence would expect 25 times 0.6, which is 15 to come true. The team got 20, which is 5 more than that, so the team is overconfident by 5 events on this set. The gap is the calibration error, and its direction is the diagnosis: a systematic shortfall against the base rate is overconfidence rather than pessimism. Calibration is a property of the whole set of forecasts, not of any one of them, so no individual forecast reveals whether the forecaster is well calibrated.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of forecasts by the stated confidence to get the calibrated expectation.

questions.explanation: A calibrated estimate is the figure that the usual overrun turns into the observed average, so it is 100 divided by one and a quarter, which is 80 days: 80 times 1.25 is exactly 100. The bias is 20 days. Applying the overrun in the wrong direction, by taking 75 percent of the average, gives 75 days, and applying it forwards to get an estimate of 125 days, are both common and both wrong, because the overrun is a property of the estimate and not of the outcome.
questions.hint: The overrun applies to the estimate, so divide the observed average by one plus the overrun.
questions.learningObjective: back out a calibrated estimate from a known overrun rate

questions.explanation: Self-serving attribution splits the credit for a good outcome and the blame for a bad one along the line of whether the outcome reflects the person rather than the circumstances. Unlike the fundamental attribution error, which concerns explaining other people's behaviour, this one concerns explaining one's own, and the asymmetry is in the person's favour. It matters for firms because reported causes determine where resources go: a team that attributes a good quarter to its own judgement will keep spending the way it did, whether or not the judgement was what produced the result.
questions.hint: Ask who receives the credit and who receives the blame.

questions.explanation: The last 3 people all act on the public action, so the share is 3 over 5, which is 0.6, while the first 2 decide on their own signals, which is 0.4. The interesting part is that the cascade runs on no new information: the followers are discarding signals they hold, and the direction of the whole group is set by the first 2 decisions, which is under half of it. Because each follower adds nothing, the group can end up confidently on the wrong side whenever those early signals point the wrong way, and it stays there for as long as the signals remain ambiguous enough to be overruled.

questions.explanation: A departure that recurs with the same sign and magnitude across many settings is a fact about behaviour rather than about one occasion, and the standard response is to restate the prediction under a better assumption. That is not a licence to discard the model: the departure identifies which assumption fails and in which direction, and a modification that reproduces the sign and the size across all of the settings is evidence that the mechanism is understood rather than merely fitted. What the evidence does not license is replacing the assumption without checking whether the new one is itself testable.
questions.hint: Ask whether the pattern is a property of the world or of one sample.
questions.learningObjective: state what a systematic departure from a model's prediction does and does not establish

options.text: Nothing at all, since predictions are never statements about real behaviour
options.misconception: denies that a theory makes a claim about behaviour

options.text: The standard assumption is wrong in a systematic way, so predictions should be restated for it
The standard assumption is wrong in that setting only, so the theory survives untouched elsewhere
options.misconception: treats a repeated pattern as a local accident
